pages.summary: Arrays into cell arrays and back: each element in a cell, cells joined into one array, and an array divided into blocks.
body: `num2cell(A)` puts each element in a cell of its own (or, with `dims`, each slice along those dimensions). `cell2mat` joins the contents of a cell array into one array; the cells must fit together as blocks. `mat2cell(A, rowSizes, colSizes)` divides an array into blocks of those sizes.

examples.title: Columns, and blocks
examples.output:
ans = 

  1×3 cell array

    {3×1 double}    {3×1 double}    {3×1 double}

ans =

     3     2

pages.summary: Each element of a cell array shown with its index.
body: Nested cells are shown element by element, with indices like `C{2}{1}`. A name to show in place of the variable's may be given.

pages.summary: A struct array from a cell array and field names, and the field values of a struct as a cell array.
body: `cell2struct(C, fields, dim)` makes a field from each element along dimension `dim` (rows with 1, columns with 2). `struct2cell` gives a cell for each field, one column per element of a struct array.

examples.title: Fields from rows, and back
examples.output:
ans = 

  struct with fields:

    name: 'Alan'
    born: 1912

ans = 

  2×1 cell array

    {'Ada'}
    {[1815]}

pages.summary: A struct's fields removed, set, read and put in order, as functions.
body: `setfield(s, name, value)` and `getfield(s, name)` are `s.(name) = value` and `s.(name)`. `rmfield` removes one field or a list. `orderfields` sorts the fields alphabetically, or in the order of another struct, a cell of names or a permutation; `perm` gives the old positions.

examples.title: A small record, edited
examples.output:
ans =

     2

s = 

  struct with fields:

    alpha: 2
     beta: 4
     zeta: 1

perm =

     2
     3
     1

pages.summary: A function called on every field of a scalar struct.
body: The results are collected in a column, one per field, when each is a single value; with `'UniformOutput', false`, as a struct with the same fields.

ans =

    a: [2 4 6]
    b: [20 40]
    c: 10

pages.summary: Keys and the values they stand for, in the order they were put in.
body: `d(keys)` looks keys up; `d(keys) = values` puts them in, giving a new dictionary (it is a value, not a handle: a copy is apart); `d(keys) = []` takes them out; `d{keys}` gives the contents of cell values. Keys are text (kept as strings), numbers or logical values; the values are all of one class. An empty `dictionary()` gets its types from what is first put in.
syntax: From arrays of keys and values.

examples.title: Prices by fruit
examples.output:
d = 

  dictionary (string ⟼ double) with 3 entries:

    "apple" ⟼ 3.5000
    "pear" ⟼ 4
    "plum" ⟼ 6

ans =

     4

ans =

    3.5000    5.0000

ans =

  1×3 string array

    "apple"    "pear"    "kiwi"

pages.summary: A dictionary's entries put in, looked up with a fallback, counted, and listed; and its types.
body: `insert` gives a dictionary with keys and values put in (`'Overwrite', false` keeps values already there). `lookup` gives the values of keys, or `FallbackValue` for keys it does not have instead of an error. `numEntries` counts the keys, `isConfigured` says whether the key and value types are set, `types` gives them, and `entries` lists the keys and values as a table (or a struct array, or a cell).

examples.title: An inventory
examples.code:
d = dictionary();
isConfigured(d)
d = insert(d, ["bolts" "nuts"], [120 300]);
[isConfigured(d) numEntries(d)]
[kt, vt] = types(d)
lookup(d, ["nuts" "screws"], FallbackValue=0)
entries(d)
examples.output:
ans =

  logical

   0

ans =

     1     2

kt =

    "string"

vt =

    "double"

ans =

   300     0

ans = 

  2×2 table

      Key      Value
    _______    _____

    "bolts"     120
    "nuts"      300

pages.summary: A map from keys (text or numbers) to values: a handle, so copies share it.
body: `M(key)` reads and sets values; `M.Count` is the number of keys; `keys`, `values`, `isKey` and `remove` work on it. The keys are kept sorted. The values may be of any kind unless `'ValueType'` limits them. A map is a handle: assigning it to another variable gives the same map, and a change through either is seen by both.
syntax: From cells (or arrays) of keys and values.

examples.title: Capitals, and a shared handle

pages.summary: The keys and values of a map or a dictionary, whether it has a key, and keys removed.
body: For a `containers.Map`, `keys` gives the keys sorted as a cell row and `values` the values in that order (or those of some keys); `remove` takes keys out of the map itself. For a `dictionary`, keys and values come in the order they were put in, as columns, and `remove` gives a new dictionary without them. `isKey` answers for one key or several.
syntax: Keys taken out of a map.

pages.summary: Inputs copied to outputs: one each, or one to all.
body: `[a, b] = deal(x, y)` is `a = x; b = y`; `[a, b] = deal(x)` gives both x. With a struct array or a cell array, `[s.field] = deal(v)` sets a field of every element. In an anonymous function, deal returns several outputs.
